title: A New, Bold Antarctic Rescue: Bringing Shackleton’s Outpost Back to Life
summary: An abandoned station manager’s villa — the site of a historic effort to save the explorer’s marooned crew — has now been restored. Take a tour inside.

Members of the South Georgia Heritage Trust restored the manager’s villa of the whaling town where the Antarctic explorer Ernest Shackleton found help for his stranded crew in 1916 and arranged their rescue.

By

Nov. 17, 2026


Updated 9:14 a.m. ET


Once a bustling whaling station, the Antarctic town of Stromness, South Georgia, has sat abandoned for more than half a century. Sixty-five harsh winters have passed since the whalers stationed there went home, reducing the empty buildings to dilapidated shacks seen from afar by passing cruise ship passengers. Seals and seabirds are the only regular inhabitants now.


But recently, there has been a burst of activity at the station. Over the past year, about a dozen people have been on a mission to save the building that was once the station manager’s villa — and the orchestration site of an elaborate plan in 1916 to save the crew of one of the era’s foremost Antarctic explorers, Ernest Shackleton.


In 1915, Shackleton and his crew were shipwrecked near a tiny landform known as Elephant Island. The nearest help was almost 800 miles away, in Stromness, so Shackleton boarded a lifeboat with his crew members Frank Worsley and Tom Crean to try and reach the way station for help. Shackleton documented the perilous trip in his autobiography, “South,” noting that the three were soaked with freezing water and starving by the time they crossed over the mountains to Stromness.


Image


One of Shackleton’s crew members with the expedition’s dogs on a foraging expedition after the crew’s ship, Endurance, was trapped in ice in 1916.


Credit...


Frank Hurley/Underwood & Underwood, via Library of Congress


Elephant Island, where the crew remained while Shackleton sought help; launching the James Caird, a small lifeboat to seek help, from Elephant Island on April 24, 1916.


Credit...


Frank Hurley/Underwood & Underwood, via Library of Congress


“Shivering with cold, yet with hearts light and happy, we set off towards the whaling-station, now not more than a mile and a half distant,” Shackleton[wrote of the final approach](https://archive.org/details/cu31924032382529/page/206/mode/2up) . “The difficulties of the journey lay behind us.”
